# Answer key - Chapter 02: Data centres, virtualisation and Linux {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-02-traffic-geography · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The chapter explains that east–west traffic dominates and that a tree forces
it through root links of fixed capacity; leaf–spine connects every leaf to
every spine so any server reaches any other over an equal-cost path
(@sec-02-traffic-geography). Options a and c describe other data-centre
concerns (they do not motivate leaf–spine), and d contradicts multi-tenancy.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-02-popek-goldberg · basic)* - **Correct: a.**
Popek and Goldberg: a machine is cleanly virtualisable only if the sensitive
instructions are a subset of the privileged ones, so every state-revealing or
state-disturbing instruction traps and can be emulated. Option b is the slow
interpreter the criterion avoids, c is para-virtualisation (which sidesteps
the criterion), d is not part of the criterion.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-02-virtualisation · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
Full virtualisation is named as the cloud default: the guest runs unmodified,
almost all instructions execute directly, only privileged operations trap
(@sec-02-virtualisation). Emulation interprets everything (slow),
para-virtualisation modifies the guest, and containers virtualise the OS,
not the hardware.

**Q4** *(tests @sec-02-linux-four-pillars · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"CPU, memory, disk, network - plus logs", "CPU, memory, disk and network;
logs complement them" (any phrasing naming all four pillars; the fifth
source is logs / `journalctl`).

**Q5** *(tests @sec-02-popek-goldberg · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"Code breaks out of its guest VM into the hypervisor, so every guest above
it is exposed", "an attacker escapes the virtual machine into the hypervisor
and can reach the other tenants' guests" (must name breaking out of the
guest into the hypervisor and the exposure of the other guests; the mild
counterpart is the noisy neighbour).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-02-distributed-system · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
Multi-tenancy is the chapter's name for many customers (tenants) using the
same physical hardware - the resource pooling of the cloud definition
(@sec-02-distributed-system). Option d is multi-cloud, a different concept
from later in the chapter; a and c describe scale and geography, not tenancy.

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-02-linux-four-pillars · applied)* -
**Model answer:** Disk filling fast: revealed by `df -h` (directory-level
detail with `du -sh`); possible log flooding or data being staged for
exfiltration. Unexpected listening port: revealed by `ss -tulpn`; a service
nobody started. The baseline matters because "before something abnormal can
be recognised, normal must be known": only comparison against the recorded
healthy values shows these as deviations rather than normal behaviour.
Threat–risk–control questions (one per observation), e.g.: "What threat
could explain this deviation (exfiltration staging / an attacker-installed
service), how likely is it and what would its impact be, and which control
would reduce that risk?" **Grading notes:** full credit needs the two
correct commands, the explicit role of the baseline, and a
threat–risk–control formulation for each observation; partial credit for
commands plus baseline reasoning without the TRC vocabulary.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-02-north-south-east-west - North–south vs east–west traffic)*
North–south: data centre $\leftrightarrow$ outside world; east–west:
server $\leftrightarrow$ server inside. East–west dominates (services call
services, replication, remote storage); leaf–spine fabrics give any-to-any
capacity.

(2) *(@exr-02-hypervisor-types - Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisors)*
Type 1 runs on bare metal (ESXi, Xen, Hyper-V), beneath every
rented cloud VM; Type 2 runs on a host OS (VMware Workstation, VirtualBox),
beneath the laboratory's Ubuntu VM.

(3) *(@exr-02-isolation-security - Isolation as a security property)*
Because tenants are strangers sharing hardware and only hypervisor mediation
separates them. Mild failure: noisy neighbour; worst case: VM escape, after
which every guest is exposed.

(4) *(@exr-02-which-command - Which command for which question)*
`ss -tulpn`; `free -h`; `journalctl` (for example `journalctl -u ssh`).

(5) *(@exr-02-blast-radius - Blast radius of one zone)*
It survives failures inside other zones only; a zone-level failure (power,
cooling, network of its own zone) takes it down. First change: spread across
availability zones; regional disasters then motivate the region pair.
